title: Match review: turn every match into a training goal
summary: After every match, a 10-minute review shows you what went well, what kept happening and what to work on next.

sections.h: Every match is information, not just a result
p: Winning doesn't always mean you played well, and losing doesn't always mean you played badly. But every match tells you something about how you played. This lesson shows you how to turn that into a training goal.

Picture two players who both lose. The first only thinks they played terribly. The second notices they struggled with high balls to the backhand, made poor choices when pulled wide and lost focus after unforced errors.
Same result, but the second player has something to take into training. The examples here are from tennis, but the same method works in padel.
sections.callout: After every match, don't just ask if you won or lost. Ask: what did this match teach me?

p: When you review a match, check these four areas one at a time:
list: Technical: which shots worked, and which caused problems?
Tactical: did you make good decisions? Did your game plan work?
Physical: could you keep your movement and intensity up to the end?
Mental: how did you handle pressure, mistakes and big points?
sections.callout: Not every missed shot is a technique problem. Maybe you were off balance, got there late, picked the wrong shot or rushed under pressure.

sections.h: Look for patterns, not one mistake
p: One missed forehand doesn't mean your forehand is weak. Maybe you were moving backwards, got a tough ball or went for a winner from the wrong spot.
Instead of single mistakes, look for the ones that keep coming back. Ask yourself:
list: Did this problem happen several times?
In what situation did it usually happen?
Was it linked to the type of ball, the opponent or the score?
Did it get worse as the match went on?
sections.callout: “My backhand was bad today” is vague. “I kept missing high balls to my backhand when I was defending from the baseline” tells you where to start. In padel the same problem might be high balls coming off the back glass.

p: In one study, experienced coaches who watched a match remembered only about 6 in 10 key moments correctly. We found no study on players' own memory, but yours won't be perfect straight after a match either.
So if you can, use these:
list: Video of the match, even a few minutes on a phone.
Simple stats, like errors on each shot.
Notes or feedback from your tennis coach.
Your own notes, on the day of the match.
sections.callout: The sooner you write it down, the less you forget. But write it once you've calmed down, not while you're still angry.

p: Once you've found a problem that keeps coming back, decide what you want to improve. Sport psychology usually splits goals into three types:

A 2022 review of 27 studies found that setting goals improves sports performance. Process goals had by far the biggest effect, and outcome goals on their own did almost nothing. A goal has to fit the player and what they need.
So don't stop at “I want a better backhand”. Make it specific: “I want to stay balanced on high backhands, hit them with more control and get back to a good court position.”
list: Outcome goal: a result measured against others, like winning a tournament.
Performance goal: a measurable improvement in your own game, like fewer backhand errors.
Process goal: something you do while you play, like keeping good spacing on high backhands.
sections.callout: A process goal is about what you control. That's why it's the most useful one in everyday training.

p: A good goal changes what you do on court. Some examples:
Your first explanation isn't always right. A backhand that breaks down could be technique, fatigue, positioning or a bad decision, and your tennis coach can help you find the real cause.
The sessions in this course are done as written. Technical, tactical and mental goals belong in tennis practice, so don't add sets or exercises to your S&C sessions.
list: Trouble with high backhands: high-ball feeding, technique and positioning, with your tennis coach.
Poor decisions when pulled wide: decision-making drills, shot choice and recovering to a good position.
Fading late in matches: the course sessions as written, including court conditioning, and the lesson “Tennis fitness”.
Losing focus after mistakes: a set routine between points, breathing and practice under pressure.
sections.warn: If what you noticed in the match is pain, not a weakness, it isn't a training goal. Read the lesson “Pain or soreness? And the red flags”.
sections.callout: Pick training that targets the real problem. More training isn't always better training.

sections.h: One or two priorities, then the next match
p: After a review you might find five or six things. Don't work on them all at once. Pick one or two using these three questions:

A high backhand that keeps losing you points is a better priority than the odd double fault. In your next match, check whether you spot high balls earlier, get into a better position and hit the shot more consistently.
You can lose the next match and still have made real progress. What matters is whether you used what you practised.
list: Impact: how much does this problem hurt your performance?
Frequency: how often does it happen in a match?
Trainability: can practice really improve it?
sections.callout: The cycle: compete, review, set a goal, train, compete again, review again.

p: After every match, take 10 minutes and answer these six questions. Keep your answers in a notebook or on your phone, and after a few matches you'll see patterns one match never shows.
ol: What went well? Write down two strengths.
What were the biggest problems? One or two specific ones.
When did they happen? Think about the score, the opponent, the type of ball and the situation.
What might have caused them? Technique, tactics, body or mind.
What's the main priority? The one that would make the biggest difference.
What will I do in my next practice? One specific thing I can actually do.
sections.callout: Ten minutes, six questions, one clear thing for your next practice.

p: Straight after a match, especially a loss, a player usually isn't ready to analyse it. These suggestions are the course's own practical advice, not a study result:
list: Wait until they've calmed down. The review doesn't have to happen in the car straight after.
Let the player answer the questions and speak first.
Ask questions instead of giving verdicts, like “where did you find it hardest?”.
Notice effort and whether they used their goal, not just the score.
Leave technique and tactics to the tennis coach.
sections.callout: Your job is to help them learn, not to judge the match.
